chapters.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood.md
chapters.relation: Karen Hoffman traces the gun across Eastwood's career as an evolving argument about violence: Dirty Harry's .44 Magnum ends violence without cost to the shooter, High Plains Drifter and Pale Rider treat the gun as righteous retribution and a proof of masculine honor, but Unforgiven shows William Munny killing men who may not deserve it and dwelling on how killing brutalizes the shooter. In Gran Torino Walt Kowalski finally gives up the gun entirely, walking unarmed into Spider's gang and being gunned down in a Christlike pose so that Thao is spared both victimhood and the guilt of killing. The chapter argues Eastwood shifts from celebrating the gun as physical protection to warning of the psychological damage violence inflicts on its user.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood.md
chapters.relation: Knight and McKnight use Northrop Frye's master genres to chart Eastwood's move from romance (the superior hero who defends a community, as Jed Cooper in Hang 'Em High, the Stranger in High Plains Drifter, Harry Callahan in Dirty Harry) toward tragedy with Mystic River, where Jimmy Markum kills the innocent Dave as his daughter's murderer and, like Oedipus, recognizes his error too late. They read the law-versus-justice tension through Aristotle's point in the Nichomachean Ethics that the lawful and the just are not coterminous, and cite McClelland glossing Walt Kowalski's self-sacrifice in Gran Torino as a supreme instance of Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis) that solves multiple problems at once.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood.md
chapters.relation: Richard McClelland analyzes Eastwood's deployment of silence in Hereafter, cataloguing four types (from long soundless episodes during Marie's near-death experience to musical rests) and grounding them in neuroscience showing the auditory cortex represents silence as an object and spontaneously fills silence with self-generated signals. He argues Eastwood intuits how silence modulates attention and memory, limiting salient characters (Marie, George, the twins) so viewers attend to and remember key emotional beats. The chapter proposes 'neurocinematics' and a 'practical realism' whereby Eastwood's laconic, minimalist style and silences latch onto real, cross-cultural features of human cognition rather than merely subjective response.

chapters.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood.md
chapters.relation: McClelland opens with the Buddha's claim that all life is suffering and reads Eastwood's aging-hero films (The Eiger Sanction, Firefox, Unforgiven, In the Line of Fire, Blood Work, Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, Gran Torino) as grounding two opposed inductions on the meaning of loss. The 'pessimistic induction' holds that many losses—Maggie's paralysis, Dave Boyle's abuse, Munny's dead—are irremediable, supporting an Aristotelian view that death dissolves the person with the body. The 'optimistic induction' draws on the science of ecological resilience to argue losses can be navigated with others' help; Walt's autonomous, meaning-making death exemplifies resilience. Hereafter's agnosticism about survival leaves Eastwood's own verdict on surviving death as 'I don't know.'

chapters.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood.md
chapters.relation: Douglas McFarland argues that Hereafter is philosophical in Nehamas's sense of an 'art of living': its three characters (Marie, George, the boy Marcus) must fashion meaning in the face of absence and abandonment rather than settle the existence of an afterlife. He aligns their struggles with Augustine's grief over his mother's death in the Confessions, Montaigne's 'I portray not being but becoming' and his revision of Socrates' Phaedo claim that philosophy is practice for death, and Sartre's view that God's absence grounds the freedom to make meaning through work. George's turn from listening to the dead to genuinely seeing the living Marcus, and his letter to Marie, mark authentic self-fashioning in the here and now.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood.md
chapters.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.
